issues.issue: The clause supersedes only prior agreements "containing general terms and conditions for repurchase transactions", a qualified formula that is not a true integration clause and leaves other prior dealings untouched. Which earlier documents survive is left open.

Annex I paragraph 15 states that this Agreement "covers all Transactions in effect as of the date hereof between the parties", which pulls pre-existing trades into the new terms that this supersession clause addresses only obliquely. The two provisions have to be read together to know what survived.

Treating every provision as "separate and independent" is in tension with Paragraph 12 and Annex I paragraph 8, which declare all Transactions and agreements a single, indivisible business relationship. A party invoking severability against netting would raise that tension.

Termination is by written notice yet "this Agreement shall, notwithstanding such notice, remain applicable to any Transactions then outstanding", so termination has no practical effect while trades remain open. What termination accomplishes, and when the relationship actually ends, is left unclear.

Requiring every modification and waiver to be "in writing and duly executed by both of the parties" sits against Paragraph 13, which permits notices, demands and requests to be made orally, and against Paragraph 3(a)'s oral Transactions. Whether a course of oral dealing altered margin practice would engage that conflict.

"[N]o material adverse change in Seller's financial condition" is a deemed representation with no defined measure of materiality, and 11(vi) turns any untrue representation into an Event of Default. The trigger is therefore judgment-laden.

The preamble recites a Master Repurchase Agreement "dated as of September 20, 1997" while the Agreement it supplements is dated as of September 20, 1998 — a date error going to which instrument the Annex attaches to. It also omits a comma before "the provisions", though that is harmless.

The Annex's blanket priority over conflicting provisions of the Agreement must be squared with Annex I paragraph 3's separate rule that a Confirmation prevails over the Agreement, producing a three-tier hierarchy nowhere fully stated. Ranking Agreement, Annex and Confirmation is left to construction.

This states flatly that all Transactions are sales and purchases, while Paragraph 6 provides for a deemed pledge and security interest if they are instead deemed loans, and Annex I paragraph 8 grants a security interest outright. The characterisation of the trades is left genuinely unsettled across these provisions.

This amended sentence gives a Confirmation priority over the Agreement, the exact reverse of the last sentence of Paragraph 3(b), which remains in the printed instrument. A dispute over a Confirmation term inconsistent with the Agreement would require choosing between them.

The default-interest sentence invokes "the LIBOR Rate" and "the third Business Day", neither of which is defined anywhere in the Agreement or Annex I. The rate and the start date for accrual therefore cannot be fixed from the text.

The forfeiture is triggered by failure to perform "any tax covenant provided for hereunder", with the covenant itself qualified by "reasonably satisfactory" and "reasonably requested". Whether a tax form was adequate enough to preserve gross-up rights is left to argument.

The Tax Event notice is "treated as a demand pursuant to paragraph 3(c)", but 3(c) governs only Transactions terminable upon demand, so its application to a fixed-term Transaction is not provided for. Fixing the effective Repurchase Date for a fixed-term trade requires reconciling the two.

Limb (ii) turns on "a substantial likelihood" that an additional amount will be payable, a threshold with no defined content, and the three limbs are misnumbered with two labelled "(ii)". Either feature makes the trigger for unilateral early termination contestable.

The clause uses "Defaulting Party" as a capitalised defined term, but the Agreement defines only a lower-case "defaulting party" in Paragraph 11, so the indemnity's trigger has no defined referent. The scope of the enforcement-costs indemnity depends on it.
"[A]ny stamp, registration, documentation or similar tax" ends in a catch-all whose reach beyond the three enumerated charges is undefined. The indemnity in 5(e) rides on that boundary.

The eligibility restriction operates "[n]otwithstanding any provision contained in this Agreement or in any additional terms or conditions contained in the Confirmation", which cuts against Annex I paragraph 3's rule that a Confirmation prevails over the Agreement. Which override wins for an ineligible security is unresolved.

Confirmation is assigned to CSFB Corporation as Agent, whereas Paragraph 3(b) requires "Buyer or Seller (or both), as shall be agreed" to deliver the Confirmation. Whose confirmation counts as the operative one is a point of construction.

The Agent is made responsible for issuing confirmations "in compliance with Rule 15c3-1", the net capital rule, where the confirmation rule is Rule 10b-10; the cross-reference does not match the duty described. "Rule [5a-6" is likewise misrendered.

The fallback makes Buyer's own affiliate — "CREDIT SUISSE FIRST BOSTON (HONG KONG) LIMITED or one of its affiliates" — the pricing source whenever "a price is not available" from the three named services, with no test for unavailability. This one-sided allocation of the valuation power is what a valuation dispute would be fought over.

It displaces Paragraph 2(j)'s requirement of a "generally recognized source agreed to by the parties" for Market Value, and its relationship to Paragraph 11(d)'s separate pricing regime for default liquidations is not stated. Which source governs which calculation must be construed.

The replacement Paragraph 12 extends the single-relationship premise to "all transactions and agreements between them", not merely Transactions hereunder as original Paragraph 12 provided, and the superseded text remains printed in the instrument. The scope of the single-agreement concept is therefore contestable.

The setoff right reaches "any other amounts or obligations owing in respect of any other agreement or transaction whatsoever", an unbounded formula with no enumerated limits. Whether obligations unconnected with repo trading fall within it is exactly what "whatsoever" leaves open.

The grant covers property transferred "pursuant to this Agreement or otherwise", and the enforcement route cites "Paragraph 11(d)()" with an empty sub-reference. Both the collateral pool and the enforcement mechanism are left indeterminate.

An outright grant of a security interest in all transferred securities is difficult to reconcile with Paragraph 6 and Annex I paragraph 2, which state that Transactions are sales and purchases and create a pledge only if they are deemed loans. The characterisation of the transfers is left inconsistent.

The notice must be given "at or prior to 10:00 am (New York Time) on such business day", but the only business day previously mentioned is the one this sentence excludes, so the operative day has no antecedent. The timing of a valid substitution notice cannot be fixed from the words.

The unilateral substitution right sits against Paragraph 9(a), under which substitution requires Buyer's "agreement with and acceptance", and against 9(b)'s deemed acceptance for Seller-custody trades. Which consent regime applies to a given Transaction requires harmonising the three.

The amount payable is whatever Buyer's "actual cost" plus a loss figure "solely determined and calculated by Buyer in good faith" comes to, with no methodology and no verification right for Seller. Both the components and the good-faith constraint invite argument.

The absolute bar on "INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, SPECIAL OR CONSEQUENTIAL" loss cannot easily be squared with Paragraph 11(g), which expressly makes a defaulting party liable for hedge-termination costs and any other loss arising from an Event of Default. A damages claim after default would put the two directly against each other.

The clause submits to "EXCLUSIVE JURISDICTION" yet only "SOLELY FOR THE PURPOSE OF" enforcement suits, so whether it forecloses proceedings elsewhere is genuinely open. Exclusivity and a purpose-limited submission pull in different directions.

The single sentence says the Agreement "covers all Transactions in effect as of the date hereof" without saying whether it displaces the terms on which those trades were originally struck. Retroactive coverage of open trades is left unexplained.

It must be read with Paragraph 14, which supersedes only prior agreements "containing general terms and conditions for repurchase transactions", leaving the status of trade-specific prior terms for existing Transactions unresolved. The two together do not say what governs an open pre-existing trade.
